precision-references.title: Choose a shunt resistor
precision-references.prompt: A 2.048 V shunt needs 150 μA, the load needs 80 μA, and supply ranges from 2.7 to 3.3 V. Find the maximum feed resistance and the high-supply no-load reference current for 2.7 kΩ.
precision-references.hint: Use minimum supply for the current guarantee; maximum supply with no load for stress.

solution.text: The upper resistance is (2.7 − 2.048)/230 μA = 2.835 kΩ. At 3.3 V a 2.7 kΩ feed supplies 463.7 μA. Check resistor tolerance, reference voltage tolerance and maximum permitted current.

precision-references.title: Reference drift in codes
precision-references.prompt: A 12-bit ADC uses 2.5 V. The reference changes by +60 ppm while a fixed input is at 75% of nominal span. Estimate the code change.
precision-references.hint: Reference error scales the code with the opposite sign.

solution.text: Nominal code is approximately 3072; its change is −3072 × 60 ppm = −0.1843 code. The input-referred voltage error is −112.5 μV. The digital output may or may not change by one code depending on its distance to a transition.

precision-references.title: Size a first-pass reservoir
precision-references.prompt: A reference charge impulse is 80 pC. What ideal capacitance limits its immediate droop to 20 μV? Why is this not a complete design?
precision-references.hint: Use charge conservation before adding the drive impedance.

solution.text: C ≥ 80 pC / 20 μV = 4 μF. Check effective capacitance under bias, ESR/ESL, recovery before the next conversion and reference-buffer stability. An ideal capacitor-only calculation omits those constraints.

precision-noise-grounding.title: Integrate a real low-pass
precision-noise-grounding.prompt: A flat 8 nV/√Hz density passes through a unity first-order 200 Hz low-pass. Find rms noise.
precision-noise-grounding.hint: Its noise bandwidth is larger than its −3 dB bandwidth.

solution.text: The equivalent bandwidth is π × 200 / 2 = 314.16 Hz. Noise is 8 × √314.16 = 141.8 nV rms.

precision-noise-grounding.title: A fast shared inductance
precision-noise-grounding.prompt: A 20 nH common return carries a current that rises by 0.25 A in 25 ns. Find the induced voltage.
precision-noise-grounding.hint: Use di/dt, not switching repetition frequency.

solution.text: 20 nH × 0.25 A / 25 ns = 0.2 V. Its effect depends on which sensitive terminals share this path; reduce loop/shared inductance.

precision-noise-grounding.title: Leakage in a current measurement
precision-noise-grounding.prompt: A 1 TΩ path from 3 V to a virtual-ground input feeds a 10 GΩ feedback resistor. Calculate output error; repeat with a guard at 3 mV.
precision-noise-grounding.hint: The guard changes voltage across the unwanted insulation.

solution.text: Ungarded leakage is 3 pA, giving 30 mV magnitude. With 3 mV across the same insulation, leakage is 3 fA and output error 30 μV. Guard-driver leakage and noise must also be budgeted.

precision-calibration.title: Invert a measured line
precision-calibration.prompt: At 0.1 V a meter reads 2100 counts; at 2.1 V it reads 42100 counts. What corrected voltage corresponds to 17100 counts?
precision-calibration.hint: Fit slope and intercept, then invert.

solution.text: Slope is 20000 counts/V. Intercept is 100 counts. The corrected result is (17100 − 100)/20000 = 0.850 V.

precision-calibration.title: Choose excitation current
precision-calibration.prompt: A 1000 Ω sensor must dissipate no more than 0.05 mW. What current limit follows?
precision-calibration.hint: Power depends on the square of current.

solution.text: I ≤ √(0.05 mW / 1000 Ω) = 223.6 μA. Check resistance at the hottest operating point and the sensor’s thermal mounting.

precision-calibration.title: Separate sensor and thermal EMF
precision-calibration.prompt: A resistor measured at ±0.5 mA gives +50.007 mV and −49.993 mV. Find resistance and additive EMF.
precision-calibration.hint: Difference isolates the odd component; sum isolates the even component.

solution.text: Resistance is 100.000 Ω from 100.000 mV / 1 mA. Additive EMF is 7 μV. This assumes equal current magnitude and no drift between readings.
